Source: https://transportation.libanswers.com/faq/154783
Title: How do I access Airline On-Time Statistics?
Chunks: 0,1,2,3,4,5,6
### Sources of Airline On-Time Statistics


### There are several ways to access statistics on on-time performance, delays, and cancelations.
* * *

### Prepared Tables
*   Airline On-Time Statistics Press Releases

*   Air Travel Consumer Reports by carrier and airport (including mishandled-baggage statistics)

*   Airline On-Time data tables (arrival and departure performance rankings)
* * *

### Simple Searches
*   On-Time Performance - Flight Delays at a Glance by year and month

*   Airline On-Time Statistics and Delay Causes
* * *

### Detailed Statistics
Access detailed data on the TranStats platform:
On the left side under "Data Finder"select "Aviation" for a list of aviation databases
Under the main column "Data Library: Aviation" select the 5th dataset"Airline On-Time Performance Data"
Then decide if you want either the Marketing or Reporting Carrier database. Please note that there are only a few years available of Marketing Carrier data.
To view 1 or 2 fields (such as on-time arrival percentage by carrier and destination airport) or a time series, select the name of the database.
Select "Analysis" next to the field name you want to view:
To add more variables select"Crosstabs" from the left margin under "Analysis Type"or click "Time Series" to see multiple years
**Tip:**we recommend using "Unique Carrier" for your airline field
To export the dataset to Excel, click "Download Results:"
To narrow your search use the"Search the Results" box in the left margin. Separate your search terms with commas. (Example: UA,DL,WN or United,Delta,Southwest)
* * *

### Download Bulk Data
Accessthe raw data in TranStats:
*   Some fields like tail number and flight number are only available through the "Download" function

*   You can only download one month of data at a time
On the left side under "Data Finder"select "Aviation" for a list of aviation databases
Under the main column "Data Library: Aviation" select the 5th dataset"Airline On-Time Performance Data:"
To access multiple fields or search data for a specific flight, click"Download" under the description of the database:
*   Use the "Filter Geography" menu to narrow state of origin/destination.  
*   Use the "Filter Year" and "Filter Period"to narrow the date range.  
*   Select the boxes for the fields you want.   
*   Remember to select performance/summary fields (e.g. DepDelay, Canceled) along with any other fields you need, such as origin and carrier.
Select "Download" after you have completed filtering the data:
* * *

### Other Resources
*   ### 14 CFR 234- reporting requirements

*   Accounting and Reporting Directives: Scroll down under "AIRLINE SERVICE QUALITY PERFORMANCE" to see which carriers file on-time data in a particular year, how it's done, and what is included in the data.

texts.4:
### Detailed Statistics
Access detailed data on the TranStats platform:
On the left side under "Data Finder"select "Aviation" for a list of aviation databases
Under the main column "Data Library: Aviation" select the 5th dataset"Airline On-Time Performance Data"
Then decide if you want either the Marketing or Reporting Carrier database. Please note that there are only a few years available of Marketing Carrier data.
To view 1 or 2 fields (such as on-time arrival percentage by carrier and destination airport) or a time series, select the name of the database.
Select "Analysis" next to the field name you want to view:
To add more variables select"Crosstabs" from the left margin under "Analysis Type"or click "Time Series" to see multiple years
**Tip:**we recommend using "Unique Carrier" for your airline field
To export the dataset to Excel, click "Download Results:"
To narrow your search use the"Search the Results" box in the left margin. Separate your search terms with commas. (Example: UA,DL,WN or United,Delta,Southwest)
* * *
texts.5:
### Download Bulk Data
Accessthe raw data in TranStats:
*   Some fields like tail number and flight number are only available through the "Download" function

*   You can only download one month of data at a time
On the left side under "Data Finder"select "Aviation" for a list of aviation databases
Under the main column "Data Library: Aviation" select the 5th dataset"Airline On-Time Performance Data:"
To access multiple fields or search data for a specific flight, click"Download" under the description of the database:
*   Use the "Filter Geography" menu to narrow state of origin/destination.  
*   Use the "Filter Year" and "Filter Period"to narrow the date range.  
*   Select the boxes for the fields you want.   
*   Remember to select performance/summary fields (e.g. DepDelay, Canceled) along with any other fields you need, such as origin and carrier.
Select "Download" after you have completed filtering the data:
* * *

#### **Passenger Flow**
This dashboard allows users to explore passenger flows from a single origin airport to destinations served by various airlines. By default, the dashboard is set to **Washington Dulles International Airport (IAD)**, but users can select a different origin and destination airport to view its passenger flows. The visualization shows where travelers are flying and which carriers operate those routes. You can also click on a specific carrier in the bar chart to highlight all destinations served by that airline. The dashboard provides an interactive view of airline networks and route coverage across the United States.
**Note:** The data is sourced from the _T-100 Traffic – Market_ dataset and is updated on a monthly basis.

#### **Passengers by Month**
Since 2014, based on U.S. and foreign air carriers, the most passengers by year derive from domestic flights, followed by inbound international flights, and lastly outbound international flights. From 2014 to 2019 there was a steady increase in the number of domestic, outbound, and inbound international passengers. However, when the pandemic hit the U.S., the total passengers flown in 2020 reached a low of 405.7 million total passengers, a 61.9 percent decrease from 2019 to 2020. In 2021, there was an increase of 74.8 percent to 708.7 million passengers. The following year there was a 33.8 percent increase from 2021 to 2022 and a 12.3 percent increase from 2022 to 2023. By 2023, the total number of passengers flown surpassed the pre-pandemic 2019 record of 1.065 billion passengers with 1.067 billion passengers in 2023. In 2025, the number of domestic passengers and inbound international passengers fell by 1.27 and 0.22 percent respectively while the outbound international passengers grew by 0.57 percent.
Note: Numbers may not add to totals due to rounding.

#### **Seats by Month**
The total seat capacity in 2025 was 1.39 billion, which is a 1.33 percent (18 million) increase from 2024, which had 1.38 billion, which was a 4.55 percent (59 million) increase from 2023. This surpassed pre-pandemic’s 2019 record of 1.29 billion seat capacity by a difference of 19 million seats. A significant recovery after 2019 to 2020’s decrease of 45.2 percent (585.3 million) to a 709.7 million-seating capacity. The following year, in 2021, reported a percentage increase of 35.8 percent (253.9 million) to 963.7 million seating capacity.
Note: Numbers may not add to totals due to rounding.

#### **Load Factor by Month**
In this table, the load factor is a ratio of passenger miles to available seat miles. Before the pandemic, in 2019, the number of passengers reached 1 billion out of a 1.3 billion seat capacity, a load factor of 82.3 percent. The following year, in 2020, there was a 25.2 percent decrease in comparison to 2019 load factor. From 2020 to 2021, the load factor rose from 57.1 to 73.5 percent, a 16.4 percent increase in load factor. By 2024, the load factor recovered to 81.3 percent with 1.4 billion seating capacity and 1.1 billion passengers. In 2025, the load factor decreased slightly by .9 percent from 81.3 percent in 2024 to 79.4 percent in 2025.
Note: Numbers may not add to totals due to rounding.

#### **Passengers by Carrier**
The top 20 carriers transported 87.4 percent of all passengers in 2025, out of 297 U.S. and foreign air carriers. Since 2018, Southwest Airlines has remained the top contributing carrier, transporting 15.3 percent of all passengers in 2025. Followed by American Airlines (15.1%), Delta Airlines (15.0%), and United Airlines (13.2%) for 2025. Southwest Airlines decreased passengers by 0.044 percent, from 169.86 million in 2025 to 177.60 million in 2024. In fourth place for the most passengers in 2025, United Air Lines increased by 0.037 percent, from 141.1 million in 2024 to 146.32 million in 2025. Between 2025 and 2024 three of the top 20 air carriers experienced a percentage decrease in passengers: Spirit Airlines (27.5), Southwest Airlines (4.4), and American Airlines (3.7).
Note: Numbers may not add to totals due to rounding.

#### **Passengers by Airport**
In 2025, the top 20 U.S. airports handled 57.2 percent (559.7 million) of all 978.5 million domestic, outbound international, and inbound international passengers representing a 1 percent decrease compared to 2024. At these top 20 U.S. airports, domestic passengers represented 53 percent (449.7 million) of all domestic passengers. Outbound and inbound international passengers represented 85.6 percent (219.8 million) of all outbound and inbound international passengers.
Note: Numbers may not add to totals due to rounding.
Note: NAS is National Aviation System
Note for all Airline Passenger and Freight Traffic (T100) - T100 Segment Data: The Air Carrier Statistics database, also known as the T-100 data, contains domestic and international airline segment data. Certificated U.S. air carriers report monthly air carrier traffic information using Form T-100. Foreign carriers having at least one point of service in the United States or one of its territories report monthly air carrier traffic information using Form T-100(f). The data is collected by the Office of Airline Information, Bureau of Transportation Statistics. This data consists of transported passengers, transported freight, seats and departures.

#### **Passenger Flow**
This dashboard allows users to explore passenger flows from a single origin airport to destinations served by various airlines. By default, the dashboard is set to **Washington Dulles International Airport (IAD)**, but users can select a different origin and destination airport to view its passenger flows. The visualization shows where travelers are flying and which carriers operate those routes. You can also click on a specific carrier in the bar chart to highlight all destinations served by that airline. The dashboard provides an interactive view of airline networks and route coverage across the United States.
**Note:** The data is sourced from the _T-100 Traffic – Market_ dataset and is updated on a monthly basis.
texts.1:
#### **Passengers by Month**
Since 2014, based on U.S. and foreign air carriers, the most passengers by year derive from domestic flights, followed by inbound international flights, and lastly outbound international flights. From 2014 to 2019 there was a steady increase in the number of domestic, outbound, and inbound international passengers. However, when the pandemic hit the U.S., the total passengers flown in 2020 reached a low of 405.7 million total passengers, a 61.9 percent decrease from 2019 to 2020. In 2021, there was an increase of 74.8 percent to 708.7 million passengers. The following year there was a 33.8 percent increase from 2021 to 2022 and a 12.3 percent increase from 2022 to 2023. By 2023, the total number of passengers flown surpassed the pre-pandemic 2019 record of 1.065 billion passengers with 1.067 billion passengers in 2023. In 2025, the number of domestic passengers and inbound international passengers fell by 1.27 and 0.22 percent respectively while the outbound international passengers grew by 0.57 percent.
Note: Numbers may not add to totals due to rounding.
texts.2:
#### **Seats by Month**
The total seat capacity in 2025 was 1.39 billion, which is a 1.33 percent (18 million) increase from 2024, which had 1.38 billion, which was a 4.55 percent (59 million) increase from 2023. This surpassed pre-pandemic’s 2019 record of 1.29 billion seat capacity by a difference of 19 million seats. A significant recovery after 2019 to 2020’s decrease of 45.2 percent (585.3 million) to a 709.7 million-seating capacity. The following year, in 2021, reported a percentage increase of 35.8 percent (253.9 million) to 963.7 million seating capacity.
Note: Numbers may not add to totals due to rounding.
texts.3:
#### **Load Factor by Month**
In this table, the load factor is a ratio of passenger miles to available seat miles. Before the pandemic, in 2019, the number of passengers reached 1 billion out of a 1.3 billion seat capacity, a load factor of 82.3 percent. The following year, in 2020, there was a 25.2 percent decrease in comparison to 2019 load factor. From 2020 to 2021, the load factor rose from 57.1 to 73.5 percent, a 16.4 percent increase in load factor. By 2024, the load factor recovered to 81.3 percent with 1.4 billion seating capacity and 1.1 billion passengers. In 2025, the load factor decreased slightly by .9 percent from 81.3 percent in 2024 to 79.4 percent in 2025.
Note: Numbers may not add to totals due to rounding.
texts.4:
#### **Passengers by Carrier**
The top 20 carriers transported 87.4 percent of all passengers in 2025, out of 297 U.S. and foreign air carriers. Since 2018, Southwest Airlines has remained the top contributing carrier, transporting 15.3 percent of all passengers in 2025. Followed by American Airlines (15.1%), Delta Airlines (15.0%), and United Airlines (13.2%) for 2025. Southwest Airlines decreased passengers by 0.044 percent, from 169.86 million in 2025 to 177.60 million in 2024. In fourth place for the most passengers in 2025, United Air Lines increased by 0.037 percent, from 141.1 million in 2024 to 146.32 million in 2025. Between 2025 and 2024 three of the top 20 air carriers experienced a percentage decrease in passengers: Spirit Airlines (27.5), Southwest Airlines (4.4), and American Airlines (3.7).
Note: Numbers may not add to totals due to rounding.
texts.5:
#### **Passengers by Airport**
In 2025, the top 20 U.S. airports handled 57.2 percent (559.7 million) of all 978.5 million domestic, outbound international, and inbound international passengers representing a 1 percent decrease compared to 2024. At these top 20 U.S. airports, domestic passengers represented 53 percent (449.7 million) of all domestic passengers. Outbound and inbound international passengers represented 85.6 percent (219.8 million) of all outbound and inbound international passengers.
Note: Numbers may not add to totals due to rounding.

OurAirports has RSS feeds for comments, CSV and HXL data downloads for geographical regions, and KML files for individual airports and personal airport lists (so that you can get your personal airport list any time you want).
Microsoft Excel users should read the special instructions below.

## Downloads
For more intense work, we have a CSV-formatted data dump of all our airports, countries, and top-level administrative subdivisions (regions), which we update every night. You can download these files and open them with almost any spreadsheet program or import them into your own database. You can even use them to set up your own, competing airport web site if you'd like! We'd love you to give us credit, like we give credit to our sources, but you're not required to.

## Downloads
### Terms of use
All data is released to the Public Domain, and comes with no guarantee of accuracy or fitness for use.

## Downloads
### Datasets
For information about the columns and values in the datasets, please visit the data dictionary and map legend (for airport and navaid types).
Effective 3 November 2021, the download files are stored on GitHub, in the repository davidmegginson/ourairports-data. The old download links redirect to there. Cloning that repository is an alternative way to access the data.
airports.csv(12,751,638 bytes, last modified Oct 28, 2026) Large file, containing information on all airports on this site. airport-frequencies.csv(1,302,302 bytes, last modified Oct 28, 2026) Large file, listing communication frequencies for the airports in `airports.csv`. airport-comments.csv(4,685,334 bytes, last modified Oct 28, 2026) Large file, listing member comments for the airports in `airports.csv`. runways.csv(3,971,778 bytes, last modified Oct 28, 2026) Large file, listing runways for the airports in `airports.csv`. navaids.csv(1,524,931 bytes, last modified Oct 28, 2026)Large file, listing worldwide radio navigation aids.countries.csv(24,583 bytes, last modified Oct 28, 2026) A list of the world's countries. You need this spreadsheet to interpret the country codes in the airports and navaids files. regions.csv(485,265 bytes, last modified Oct 28, 2026) A list of all countries' top-level administrative subdivisions (provinces, governorates, states, etc.). You need this spreadsheet to interpret the region codes in the airport file.

## Workarounds for Microsoft Excel
The CSV files above use the Unicode UTF-8 character encoding to represent a wide range of non-English characters, such as Hellenic, Cyrillic, Han Chinese, and Arabic scripts, as well as accented Latin characters.
Unfortunately, Microsoft Excel does not detect the character encoding of CSV files, and does not allow you to specify the encoding when you open them, always assuming a proprietary Microsoft character encoding. As a result, if you simply open the CSV files in Excel, any non-English characters will be scrambled.
There are two workarounds available:
1.   Create a new, blank spreadsheet first, then use Excel's text import tool to load the CSV file into the blank spreadsheet.  
2.   Rename the CSV file's extension to ".txt" before opening it with Excel.
In both cases, Excel will give you an opportunity to specify the field separator (",") and the character encoding ("UTF-8"), and then accented and other non-English characters should appear without problem.
These workarounds are not necessary for OpenOffice Calc, which always prompts for the character encoding when opening a CSV file (just choose "UTF-8").

### Busiest U.S. airports by domestic flight volume:
These were the busiest airports in 2024:
1.   ATL - Atlanta Hartsfield International Airport - 342,624 flights

3.   DFW - Dallas/Fort Worth International Airport - 315,695 flights

5.   CLT - Charlotte/Douglas International Airport - 252,441 flights

## Highlights from the Dataset:
### Days with the most flights
Sunday after Thanksgiving was the day with the most flights in 2024 and is consistently the busiest travel day of the year. The next busiest travel days were Thursdays and Fridays in October and Fridays in July.

## Highlights from the Dataset:
### Days with the least flights
Thanksgiving day was the least busiest travel day followed by Saturdays in mid-January to mid-February.

## Highlights from the Dataset:
### Days with the most flight delays
Holiday travel stood out with the most flight delays. One of the worst days to travel was 12/29 with 47% of flights delayed 10+ mins and 12/28 and 12/21 were close behind with 41% of flights delayed 10+ min. While these days have a lot of flight delays they were below average for flights cancelled.

## Flight Dataset Summary
This spreadsheet includes 26.3 million rows of U.S. flight data from the Bureau of Transportation Statistics from 2022 to 2025. There is one row for each U.S. domestic flight.
Columns include Date, Carrier Code, Airline Name, Flight Number, Origin, Destination, Scheduled Departure, Actual Departure Time, Flight Delay (in minutes), Cancelled (flight cancellations are recorded as "1"). Note that you can download new months and additional flight data fields from the BTS TranStats website and open in Row Zero. Row Zero is a spreadsheet for big data that can easily open files too big for Excel.
**The workbook contains 4 sheets**:
*   Flight Dataset (all raw data)  
*   Example analysis  
*   Airport Code Lookup, which maps U.S. airports to their IATA codes  
*   U.S. Carrier Lookup, which maps U.S. airlines to their carrier code

## Example Analysis
View the Spreadsheet
We can quickly create a few pivot tables and charts to analyze this airline dataset.
First, we'll create a pivot table to look at total flights, flight delays, and flight cancellations by airport. We can look at delays in a few ways - mean, median, 90th percentile (gives us the 10% worst delays) using the pivot table calculations. We can also use XLOOKUP to join with another pivot table that filters to flights delayed 10+ mins. Next, we can add calculated columns onto our pivot table to see the percent of flights delayed and cancelled at U.S. airports.
We can insert a chart to better visualize the data.
Next we can look at cancels and delays by departure time to see that flights are more likely to be delayed and cancelled later in the day, whereas morning flights have the fewest delays and cancellations.
We can also look at U.S. flight delays by airline. Here we see that the median flight delay is typically less than zero, meaning the typical flight is on time. However, we can use a pivot table to calculate percentile values, to show a more interesting story. ## Workarounds for Microsoft Excel
The CSV files above use the Unicode UTF-8 character encoding to represent a wide range of non-English characters, such as Hellenic, Cyrillic, Han Chinese, and Arabic scripts, as well as accented Latin characters.
Unfortunately, Microsoft Excel does not detect the character encoding of CSV files, and does not allow you to specify the encoding when you open them, always assuming a proprietary Microsoft character encoding. As a result, if you simply open the CSV files in Excel, any non-English characters will be scrambled.
There are two workarounds available:
1.   Create a new, blank spreadsheet first, then use Excel's text import tool to load the CSV file into the blank spreadsheet.  
2.   Rename the CSV file's extension to ".txt" before opening it with Excel.
In both cases, Excel will give you an opportunity to specify the field separator (",") and the character encoding ("UTF-8"), and then accented and other non-English characters should appear without problem.
These workarounds are not necessary for OpenOffice Calc, which always prompts for the character encoding when opening a CSV file (just choose "UTF-8").

* * *

## Flight Dataset Summary
This spreadsheet includes 26.3 million rows of U.S. flight data from the Bureau of Transportation Statistics from 2022 to 2025. There is one row for each U.S. domestic flight.
Columns include Date, Carrier Code, Airline Name, Flight Number, Origin, Destination, Scheduled Departure, Actual Departure Time, Flight Delay (in minutes), Cancelled (flight cancellations are recorded as "1"). Note that you can download new months and additional flight data fields from the BTS TranStats website and open in Row Zero. Row Zero is a spreadsheet for big data that can easily open files too big for Excel.
**The workbook contains 4 sheets**:
*   Flight Dataset (all raw data)  
*   Example analysis  
*   Airport Code Lookup, which maps U.S. airports to their IATA codes  
*   U.S. Carrier Lookup, which maps U.S. airlines to their carrier code
View Spreadsheet

## Highlights from the Dataset:
### Busiest U.S. airports by domestic flight volume:
These were the busiest airports in 2024:
1.   ATL - Atlanta Hartsfield International Airport - 342,624 flights  
2.   ORD - Chicago, O'Hare International Airport - 318,173 flights  
3.   DFW - Dallas/Fort Worth International Airport - 315,695 flights  
4.   DEN - Denver International Airport - 313,314 flights  
5.   CLT - Charlotte/Douglas International Airport - 252,441 flights

## Highlights from the Dataset:
### Days with the most flights
Sunday after Thanksgiving was the day with the most flights in 2024 and is consistently the busiest travel day of the year. The next busiest travel days were Thursdays and Fridays in October and Fridays in July.

## Highlights from the Dataset:
### Days with the least flights
Thanksgiving day was the least busiest travel day followed by Saturdays in mid-January to mid-February.

## Highlights from the Dataset:
### Days with the most flight delays
Holiday travel stood out with the most flight delays. One of the worst days to travel was 12/29 with 47% of flights delayed 10+ mins and 12/28 and 12/21 were close behind with 41% of flights delayed 10+ min. While these days have a lot of flight delays they were below average for flights cancelled.

## Highlights from the Dataset:
### Largest U.S. Airlines by Flights:
These were the airlines with the most flights in 2024
1.   Southwest - 1,419,419 flights  
2.   Delta - 1,009,194 flights  
3.   American - 984,306 flights  
4.   United - 760,451 flights  
5.   SkyWest - 744,637 flights

## Highlights from the Dataset:
### Airport with the most direct flights:
DFW (Dallas Fort Worth) offered the most direct flights in 2025 with 184 direct flight destinations in the U.S. Here's the top 5 airports with most direct flights:
1.   DFW - 184  
2.   DEN - 182  
3.   ORD - 176  
4.   ATL - 158  
5.   CLT - 139

## Example Analysis
View the Spreadsheet
We can quickly create a few pivot tables and charts to analyze this airline dataset.
First, we'll create a pivot table to look at total flights, flight delays, and flight cancellations by airport. We can look at delays in a few ways - mean, median, 90th percentile (gives us the 10% worst delays) using the pivot table calculations. We can also use XLOOKUP to join with another pivot table that filters to flights delayed 10+ mins. Next, we can add calculated columns onto our pivot table to see the percent of flights delayed and cancelled at U.S. airports.
We can insert a chart to better visualize the data.
Next we can look at cancels and delays by departure time to see that flights are more likely to be delayed and cancelled later in the day, whereas morning flights have the fewest delays and cancellations.
We can also look at U.S. flight delays by airline. Here we see that the median flight delay is typically less than zero, meaning the typical flight is on time. However, we can use a pivot table to calculate percentile values, to show a more interesting story. Looking at the 90th percentile delay for each airline (p90 of Delay) shows the 10% worst flight delays for each airline. Here you can see that it's not uncommon to have flight delays over 30 mins.
We can use a unique Row Zero feature to analyze the busiest days to travel and worst days to travel. ## Flight Dataset Summary
This spreadsheet includes 26.3 million rows of U.S. flight data from the Bureau of Transportation Statistics from 2022 to 2025. There is one row for each U.S. domestic flight.
Columns include Date, Carrier Code, Airline Name, Flight Number, Origin, Destination, Scheduled Departure, Actual Departure Time, Flight Delay (in minutes), Cancelled (flight cancellations are recorded as "1"). Note that you can download new months and additional flight data fields from the BTS TranStats website and open in Row Zero. Row Zero is a spreadsheet for big data that can easily open files too big for Excel.
**The workbook contains 4 sheets**:
*   Flight Dataset (all raw data)  
*   Example analysis  
*   Airport Code Lookup, which maps U.S. airports to their IATA codes  
*   U.S. Carrier Lookup, which maps U.S. airlines to their carrier code

## Highlights from the Dataset:
### Busiest U.S. airports by domestic flight volume:
These were the busiest airports in 2024:
1.   ATL - Atlanta Hartsfield International Airport - 342,624 flights  
2.   ORD - Chicago, O'Hare International Airport - 318,173 flights  
3.   DFW - Dallas/Fort Worth International Airport - 315,695 flights  
4.   DEN - Denver International Airport - 313,314 flights  
5.   CLT - Charlotte/Douglas International Airport - 252,441 flights
texts.3:
## Highlights from the Dataset:
### Days with the most flights
Sunday after Thanksgiving was the day with the most flights in 2024 and is consistently the busiest travel day of the year. The next busiest travel days were Thursdays and Fridays in October and Fridays in July.
texts.4:
## Highlights from the Dataset:
### Days with the least flights
Thanksgiving day was the least busiest travel day followed by Saturdays in mid-January to mid-February.
texts.5:
## Highlights from the Dataset:
### Days with the most flight delays
Holiday travel stood out with the most flight delays. One of the worst days to travel was 12/29 with 47% of flights delayed 10+ mins and 12/28 and 12/21 were close behind with 41% of flights delayed 10+ min. While these days have a lot of flight delays they were below average for flights cancelled.

### Airport with the most direct flights:
DFW (Dallas Fort Worth) offered the most direct flights in 2025 with 184 direct flight destinations in the U.S. Here's the top 5 airports with most direct flights:

2.   DEN - 182

## Example Analysis
View the Spreadsheet
We can quickly create a few pivot tables and charts to analyze this airline dataset.
First, we'll create a pivot table to look at total flights, flight delays, and flight cancellations by airport. We can look at delays in a few ways - mean, median, 90th percentile (gives us the 10% worst delays) using the pivot table calculations. We can also use XLOOKUP to join with another pivot table that filters to flights delayed 10+ mins. Next, we can add calculated columns onto our pivot table to see the percent of flights delayed and cancelled at U.S. airports.
We can insert a chart to better visualize the data.
Next we can look at cancels and delays by departure time to see that flights are more likely to be delayed and cancelled later in the day, whereas morning flights have the fewest delays and cancellations.
We can also look at U.S. flight delays by airline. Here we see that the median flight delay is typically less than zero, meaning the typical flight is on time. However, we can use a pivot table to calculate percentile values, to show a more interesting story. Looking at the 90th percentile delay for each airline (p90 of Delay) shows the 10% worst flight delays for each airline. Here you can see that it's not uncommon to have flight delays over 30 mins.
